content: 1. Dual therapy is recommended over single therapy for the treatment of gonococcal infections, particularly in pregnant women, who require close monitoring for potential complications. This recommendation is based on conditional evidence of very low quality. 2. In cases of gonococcal infection treatment failure, the WHO STI guidelines suggest the following approaches: If reinfection is suspected, re-treat using a WHO-recommended regimen, emphasize sexual abstinence or consistent condom use, and ensure partner treatment. If treatment failure occurred after using a non-WHO-recommended regimen, re-treat with a WHO-recommended regimen. If treatment failure occurred and resistance data are available, re-treat according to the susceptibility profile. If treatment failure occurred after WHO-recommended single therapy, re-treat with WHO-recommended dual therapy. If treatment failure occurred after WHO-recommended dual therapy, re-treat with one of the following dual therapies: Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscularly as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose. Cefixime 800 mg orally as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose. Gentamicin 240 mg intramuscularly as a single dose plus azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose. Spectinomycin 2 g intramuscularly as a single dose (if not an oropharyngeal infection) plus azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose. 3. For neonates with gonococcal conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum), the WHO STI guidelines recommend one of the following treatment options: Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (maximum 150 mg) intramuscularly as a single dose. Kanamycin 25 mg/kg (maximum 75 mg) intramuscularly as a single dose. Spectinomycin 25 mg/kg (maximum 75 mg) intramuscularly as a single dose. 4. Neonates with gonococcal conjunctivitis should be treated due to the significant net benefit of treatment. The choice of treatment may depend on the cost, quality of the medication, and equity considerations in different settings. 5. For the prevention of both chlamydial and gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, the following topical agents are recommended: 5% povidone-iodine solution (water-based). 1% silver nitrate solution. 1% chloramphenicol eye ointment. 6. Care should be taken to avoid contact with eye tissue when applying topical treatments, and a water-based povidone-iodine solution should be used. 7. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are a significant global public health issue, causing substantial morbidity and mortality. They directly impact reproductive and child health through infertility, cancers, and pregnancy complications, and indirectly facilitate the sexual transmission of HIV, affecting both national and individual economies. 8. In 2012, an estimated 357 million new cases of curable STIs occurred among adults aged 15–49 years worldwide, including 131 million cases of chlamydia, 78 million cases of gonorrhea, 6 million cases of syphilis, and 142 million cases of trichomoniasis. 9. Viral STIs, such as herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2) and human papillomavirus (HPV), are also highly prevalent, with 417 million people infected with HSV-2 and approximately 291 million women harboring HPV at any given time. 10. Untreated curable STIs can lead to severe complications, including pelvic inflammatory disease, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, fetal loss, and congenital infections. In 2012, maternal syphilis infections resulted in 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes, including stillbirths and neonatal deaths. 11. The psychological consequences of STIs include stigma, shame, and loss of self-worth, further emphasizing the need for effective prevention and treatment strategies. 12. The WHO emphasizes the importance of updated global treatment recommendations to address changing antimicrobial resistance patterns, particularly for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Effective treatment protocols that consider global and local resistance patterns are essential to mitigate the risk of further antimicrobial resistance development. 13. High-level resistance to quinolones and decreased susceptibility to third-generation cephalosporins, previously recommended first-line treatments for gonorrhea, are on the rise. Resistance to azithromycin has also been reported in some strains of Treponema pallidum, and treatment failures have been observed with tetracyclines and macrolides in the treatment of Chlamydia trachomatis. 14. The syndromic management approach, which guides STI diagnosis based on symptom groups and signs, needs to be updated to reflect the changing epidemiology of STIs. This includes revising algorithms for genital ulcer disease and vaginal discharge and developing new algorithms for anorectal infections in key populations, such as men who have sex with men and sex workers. 15. Rapid point-of-care diagnostic tests (POCTs) are transforming STI management by enabling earlier diagnosis and treatment initiation. Updated guidelines should incorporate these tests into syndromic management and provide algorithms for testing and screening. 16. Despite advancements in diagnostics, therapeutics, vaccines, and barrier methods, access to these technologies remains limited, particularly in high-burden areas. Global guidelines must address settings with limited access to modern technologies while optimizing their use in resource-rich settings. 17. Countries are strongly encouraged to adopt updated global guidance when establishing standardized national protocols, adapting them to local epidemiological and antimicrobial susceptibility data. Standardization ensures adequate treatment at all levels of healthcare, optimizes provider training, and facilitates medicine procurement. 18. The WHO plans a phased approach to updating STI guidelines, addressing specific infections and issues in phases, including treatment, prevention, and laboratory diagnosis. Comprehensive guidelines will consolidate these phases to provide a unified approach to STI case management.
